name: Asaniah
title: Levite and Law Teacher under King Jehoshaphat
summary: Under King Jehoshaphat's religious reform program in Judah, the Levite Azariah was appointed as one of those who were to travel throughout the cities of the kingdom and teach the people the law of the Lord. In the third year of his reign, he, along with other Levites, priests, and the king's officials, was sent out with the Book of the Law of the Lord to restore and strengthen the people's knowledge of the covenant with God. This systematic teaching effort was a central element in Jehoshaphat's reforms and showed how royal authority and religious leaders worked together to renew faithfulness to the Lord. According to Chronicles, this reform work resulted in the fear of the Lord falling upon the surrounding nations, and Judah experienced a period marked by peace and growth.

keyEvents.title: Sent out to teach the people the law of the Lord
keyEvents.description: Asaniah was among the Levites whom King Jehoshaphat sent out in his third year of reign to teach the people the law of the Lord in the cities of Judah. Together with the king's officials and priests, they traveled around carrying the Book of the Law of the Lord and teaching the people. This formed a cornerstone of Jehoshaphat's religious reform program, aimed at strengthening the covenant relationship between God and his people.

keyEvents.title: Effect of the Reform: Peace and Prosperity in Judah
keyEvents.description: As a result of Jehoshaphat's faithfulness and the extensive reform work in which Asaniah and the other Levites participated, the fear of the Lord fell upon the surrounding kingdoms, so that they did not wage war against Judah. The kingdom then experienced a period of peace and prosperity.

versions.summary: Asaniah was a Levite who served under King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He was one of the Levites sent out to teach the people the law of the Lord in the cities of Judah. His service was part of Jehoshaphat's religious reform program.
versions.title: Levite in the Service of King Jehoshaphat
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Levite in King Jehoshaphat's service' is functional but could be refined. Asaiah was specifically one of the Levites who taught the law.; [major] Jehoshaphat reigned approximately 872–848 BC. Therefore, the lifespan should be adjusted; stating 'the 800s BC' is somewhat imprecise. It would be better to say 'approximately the 870s BC' or 'active around 870 BC' to reflect Jehoshaphat's third regnal year (around 869 BC).; [major] Asaiah is referred to as a Levite in 2 Chron 17:8, not as a priest. The role 'priest' is incorrect – the text distinguishes between priests (Elishama and Joram are mentioned separately as priests) and Levites. The title 'leader' is also imprecise; 'teacher' or 'law teacher' would be more accurate.; [minor] The summary is good but should clarify that he was a Levite (not a priest) and mention that he traveled together with leaders, priests, and other Levites.; [minor] The second key event (Part of Jehoshaphat's reform program) in verses 3–6 primarily concerns Jehoshaphat's own walk and his seeking the Lord, not directly the sending out of the Levites. It is context but not directly about Asaiah. Consider adjusting the description.; [minor] The third key event attributes the blessing directly to the reform program in which Asaiah participated. The text states that the fear of the Lord fell upon the kingdoms, but linking this personally to Asaiah seems somewhat exaggerated for someone mentioned so briefly.; [minor] The fourth key event is more a theological reflection than an event. It repeats much of what was already covered in the first event.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. Interesting points could include the meaning of the name, Jehoshaphat's reform program in its historical context, and the role of the Levites as teachers.

versions.summary: Asaniah was a Levite who served under King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He was one of the Levites who, together with leaders and priests, were sent out in the third year of Jehoshaphat's reign to teach the people the law of the Lord in the cities of Judah. This mission was a central part of Jehoshaphat's religious reform program, which aimed to strengthen the people's knowledge of God's law and bring them back to faithfulness to the covenant.

versions.reason: [minor] The third key event ('The Lord's blessing over Judah') does not directly concern Asaniah, but rather the general consequences of Jehoshaphat's reforms. Although it provides context, linking this directly to Asaniah's profile may be misleading. This should be clarified or possibly removed to maintain focus on Asaniah's role.; [minor] The first two key events ('Sent out to teach the law' and 'Part of Jehoshaphat's religious reform') overlap significantly in content and biblical references. Merging them or distinguishing them more clearly would strengthen the profile.; [minor] The dating 'c. 869 BC' is a reasonable approximation based on Jehoshaphat's reign, but various chronologies differ slightly. A slightly broader formulation may be more accurate, e.g., 'Active c. 870–860 BC.'; [minor] The linguistic footnote gives the Hebrew form 'עֲשַׂהְיָה' (Asahya). The Hebrew name in 2 Chr 17:8 is rather עֲשַׁהְאֵל (Asahel) or similar forms depending on the textual tradition. The form should be checked more carefully against the Hebrew base text.

versions.summary: Asania was a Levite who served under King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is mentioned as one of the Levites sent out in Jehoshaphat's third year to teach the people the law of the Lord in the cities of Judah. Together with the king's officials and priests, these Levites traveled throughout the land carrying the Book of the Law and instructing the people. This mission was an important part of Jehoshaphat's religious reform program, which aimed to renew the people's knowledge of God's law and strengthen the covenant relationship between the Lord and his people. According to Chronicles, this reform caused the fear of the Lord to fall upon the surrounding nations, and the kingdom experienced a period of peace and growth.
versions.title: Levite and Law Teacher under King Jehoshaphat
versions.reason:
[minor] The summary is well formulated but structurally resembles the two previous versions—especially the opening "Asania was a Levite who served under King Jehoshaphat of Judah." Since this is the third version, the text should clearly distinguish itself from earlier drafts with a more varied introduction and perspective.
[minor] The second key event ("Effect of the reform: Peace and prosperity in Judah") is not an event Asania was personally involved in; it is a general consequence of the entire reform program. It may be more precise either to remove this or to clarify that this is an indirect result of the work he participated in.
[minor] The Hebrew form "עֲשַׂהְיָה" (Asahya) is reasonable, but the precise Hebrew spelling of the name as it appears in 2 Chr 17:8 is debated. The form in the Masoretic text is עֲשַׂהְאֵל or similar variants depending on the manuscript. It should be noted that there is uncertainty about the exact form.
[minor] The footnotes are generally good, but the last footnote concerning "the book of the law of the Lord" touches on speculative research. It could be phrased somewhat more neutrally to reflect that there are multiple views.

footnotes.text: The name Asaniah (Hebrew: עֲשַׂהְיָה) may mean 'the Lord has done/created,' composed of the Hebrew verb 'asah' (to do, to create) and the theophoric element Yah, a short form of the divine name YHWH. Such theophoric names were very common in ancient Israel and testify to parents' gratitude and faith at the birth of their child.

Jehoshaphat's sending of Levites, priests, and leaders to teach the law (2 Chr 17:7–9) represents an early example of organized religious education for the people in Judah. This arrangement can be seen as a precursor to the teaching function that was later institutionalized in the synagogue after the exile.

According to the Mosaic Law, the Levites had a special role as guardians and mediators of God's law (Deut 33:10). During the monarchy, this role was continued through initiatives such as Jehoshaphat's reform program, where the Levites traveled with 'the Book of the Law of the Lord' to teach the people in the cities of Judah.

Jehoshaphat's reform likely took place around 870–865 BC (his third regnal year). The account of this reform in Chronicles emphasizes the close cooperation between royal authority and religious leaders—a recurring pattern in Judah's history, from Jehoshaphat through Hezekiah to Josiah.

The expression 'the Book of the Law of the Lord' (2 Chr 17:9) raises questions about which collection of texts was in circulation at that time. It may have been an early compilation of legal texts, possibly related to parts of Deuteronomy or other sections of the books of Moses, but its exact content is debated among scholars.

In rabbinic tradition, Jehoshaphat's initiative for teaching the law was seen as a model for how religious knowledge should be actively spread to all the people, not reserved only for a small elite. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 20a) mentions this type of royal initiative as an ideal for the interaction between secular power and spiritual guidance.
